sources.title: Joshua Wong biographical student handout: 13 October 1996 birth in Hong Kong
sources.findings: Read the Joshua Wong student-biography page in the RFK Human Rights classroom PDF. It explicitly gives birth in Hong Kong on 13 October 1996. This is a secondary educational biography, not a birth register. Its broader discussion of 2047 and its compressed accounts of arrests, imprisonment and appeals are not used as authoritative legal chronology. No unverified university degree, family detail, health history or present organisational office is imported.

sources.title: March–April 2015 interview, Scholarism on the March: May 2011 founding account
sources.findings: Read the accessible opening of Wong’s March–April 2015 New Left Review interview. His first-person account describes a 1996 Hong Kong birth and organising with friends in May 2011 around opposition to the proposed Moral and National Education curriculum. The exact founding month is attributed to this retrospective self-report; the whole interview beyond the accessible extract was not reviewed. His broad claims about the unprecedented nature of student participation are not independently adopted.

sources.title: 8 September 2012: national education decisions left to schools, three-year deadline removed
sources.findings: Read the Hong Kong government’s 8 September 2012 policy announcement. It removed the deadline after the three-year initiation period and left schools and school-sponsoring bodies to decide whether, how and when to introduce the subject, with curriculum guidance subject to review. This was not a permanent ban on national education or a claim that all civic education ceased. The government attributed its decision to multiple stakeholders; the public biography does not credit Wong alone with the policy change.

sources.title: 10 April 2016 Demosisto launch report: co-founders and Nathan Law as chair
sources.findings: Read Anadolu’s 10 April 2016 launch report, updated 18 April. It distinguishes Nathan Law as party chair and Wong, formerly of Scholarism, as the new organisation’s secretary, and reports proposed electoral and international-advocacy activity. Public wording uses the well-supported co-founder role rather than extending an old title to 2026. The article mistakenly places the long Occupy street protests in late 2015; this is not adopted, as the 2014 chronology is corroborated by court summaries and other reporting. Proposed referendum options, forecasts and the article’s categorical treatment of 2047 are not imported as settled constitutional outcomes.

sources.title: Summary of [2018] HKCFA 4: 6 February 2018 sentence appeals and 2014 incident
sources.findings: Read the complete short Department of Justice summary of FACC 8–10/2017, [2018] HKCFA 4. It identifies the 26 September 2014 forecourt incident, trial convictions and original 80-hour community-service order for Wong, the 17 August 2017 sentence review, and the 6 February 2018 successful appeals against sentence. Its June 2018 publication is not the judgment date. The CFA accepted that stricter guidance could apply to future cases while finding no proper basis to alter the earlier magistrate’s reasonable sentence. This is not an acquittal or a holding that all protest-related conduct is lawful. It is a departmental judgment summary, not the full original judgment.

sources.title: 6 February 2018: original community-service sentence reinstated, distinct contempt case
sources.findings: Read Human Rights Watch’s contemporaneous 6 February 2018 account, including the explicit reinstatement of Wong’s completed 80-hour community-service order and the separate Mong Kok contempt case. It corroborates the outcome of the sentencing appeal, while its normative criticism remains attributed. The other activists’ suspended sentence and service hours are not assigned to Wong. The 2018 description of bail or potential further imprisonment is not carried forward as his current legal status.

sources.title: 30 June 2020: national security law passed and Demosisto announces dissolution
sources.findings: Read Reuters’s contemporaneous 30 June 2020 report via Daily Maverick. It records passage of the national security law and Demosisto’s announcement of dissolution that day while details and commencement were still expected later. Therefore the event is not described as occurring only after the law had already taken effect. The national legislature’s enactment, an organisation’s dissolution and subsequent individual prosecutions are separate events. The article does not establish the exact hour or every member’s resignation sequence.

sources.publisher: Hong Kong Court of First Instance, copy hosted by Columbia Global Freedom of Expression
sources.title: HCCC 69/2022, [2024] HKCFI 3298: D19, paragraphs 154–161 and sentence table
sources.findings: Read selected D19 passages within paragraphs 154–161 and the final sentence table in the court’s 2024 reasons for sentence, hosted by Columbia Global Freedom of Expression. They identify Wong Chi-fung, his accepted active-participant classification, a seven-year starting point, one-third reduction for guilty plea and final four years eight months (56 months). Do not mistake D29, another defendant also sentenced to 56 months, for Wong. His 2024 mitigation did not raise mistake of law, unlike arguments made in the later 2026 case. No complete read of every defendant’s evidence or later appeal record is claimed. Direct judiciary-frame access was unavailable; the mirrored judicial PDF was readable.

sources.publisher: Hong Kong National Security Law case database
sources.title: Case summary of 19 November 2024 sentencing, identifying conspiracy charge and D19
sources.findings: Read the official national-security case summary header and background and the heading identifying D19. It confirms HCCC 69/2022, [2024] HKCFI 3298, 19 November 2024 sentencing, a conspiracy-to-commit-subversion count and the alleged plan involving a legislative majority, indiscriminate budget refusal and government paralysis. The case concerned more than the bare fact of voting in a primary. Forty-seven defendants were charged, but 45 were sentenced after guilty pleas or trial convictions; do not say all 47 were convicted on one day. The public profile does not claim Wong’s guilty plea occurred on the May 2024 trial-verdict date for other defendants.

sources.title: 6 June 2025: second national security charge and court appearance
sources.findings: Read Reuters’s 6 June 2025 court report via StreetInsider. It describes a new conspiracy-to-collude charge while Wong was already serving the primary-case sentence; the charge sheet’s period is 1 July–23 November 2020. His court response that he understood the charge is not a guilty plea. A separate police suspicion concerning property is not automatically an additional charge, conviction or part of the later sentence. The historical expected January 2027 release is superseded by the November 2026 sentence; the article’s file photo from March 2021 is not a new June 2025 photograph.

sources.title: 2 September 2026: guilty plea in foreign-collusion case
sources.findings: Read RTHK’s 2 September 2026 report of Wong’s guilty plea and mitigation, with sentencing adjourned at that stage. Prosecution references to older international-lobbying arrangements are distinct from the charged post-commencement period. The defence’s discussion of the pre-existing sentence and January 2027 expected completion does not fix his release after the later case. Do not leave this profile at the outdated awaiting-sentence stage.

sources.title: 5 November 2026: ten-year sentence and government response in Wong collusion case
sources.findings: Read the Hong Kong government’s 5 November 2026 English announcement and the central passages of its Chinese counterpart. They state that Wong pleaded guilty on 2 September and was sentenced that day to ten years for conspiracy to commit collusion under Article 29. The release reports the court’s grave-offence assessment but also includes the chief executive’s and government spokesperson’s political condemnation. Those statements are attributed government positions, not independent biographical character judgments. The full 2026 reasons for sentence were not inspected; official reporting is corroborated by RTHK and Reuters. No final outcome of a future appeal or completed asset confiscation is asserted.

sources.title: 5 November 2026: ten-year sentence, two months and two days concurrent with existing term
sources.findings: Read RTHK’s 5 November 2026 sentencing report, especially the judge’s starting point, reduction and two months plus two days concurrent with the existing subversion sentence. This is more precise than rounding concurrency to two months and rules out simply adding ten years to the full earlier term. The ten-year sentence is not described as life imprisonment. No independent prison-calculation record, remission decision or definitive release date was obtained.

sources.title: 5 November 2026: sentencing, observed appearance in court and mitigation remarks
sources.findings: Read Reuters’s 5 November 2026 courtroom report via Investing.com. It describes Wong’s actual presence and gestures in court, the delivered ten-year sentence, September plea, charged July–November 2020 conduct, mitigation remarks and government responses. The hosting site’s 4 November US-time publication label does not move the Hong Kong sentencing to 4 November. His denial of advocating independence or receiving foreign funding, and the government’s contrary political characterisations, remain attributed; the public profile does not turn either into a blanket factual description. The appearance supplies recent life-status evidence without claiming to have viewed photos or video.

sources.title: 5 November 2026: human-rights criticism of the new sentence and call for release
sources.findings: Read Human Rights Watch’s 5 November 2026 criticism and call for unconditional release. The account is a human-rights assessment, not a court order vacating convictions. Its rounded two-month overlap is less precise than RTHK’s two months and two days, and its projected late-2036 release is not copied as certain. Its compressed January 2021 charged chronology is not used to establish an exact arrest/charging date in the primary case. Distinguish NGO assessments of freedom of expression from government views of national security and from adjudicated outcomes.

sources.title: 5 November 2026 profile: student activism, Umbrella Movement and international attention
sources.findings: Read relevant passages of Reuters’s 5 November 2026 profile via Investing.com. It corroborates early Scholarism activism, the Umbrella Movement and sustained international visibility. Do not describe Wong as the sole organiser of a broad movement, confuse a magazine cover or Nobel nomination with winning an award, or adopt the profile’s loose toddler-age phrasing as a birth record. Claims that protests forced a policy change are tempered by the separately reviewed government policy text and acknowledgement of multiple participants.

Refresh appeals and custody status before publication; inspect complete original judgments and prison records before adding comprehensive legal conclusions or a definite release date.
